title: BS-PDN-Last: Towards Optimal Power Delivery Network Design With Multifunctional Backside Metal Layers
problem: Backside metal layers in advanced chips can serve multiple functions (power delivery, signal routing, thermal); traditional PDN-first design flows reserve these layers for power, leaving suboptimal signal routing and performance trade-offs.
motivation: Maximizing PPA (power, performance, area) gains with multifunctional backside requires rethinking the physical design order; conventional flows constrain the design space.
method: The traditional approach reserves backside metal layers for power delivery from the start, limiting how signal routing (the data paths between circuits) can optimize and hurting performance. BS-PDN-Last reverses this order: it lets signal routing optimize for speed and performance first by using as much backside space as needed, then fits the power delivery network into the space that remains. This reordering works because signal routing is harder to reroute than power distribution. The method uses vector-based IR-drop analysis—a calculation that predicts voltage drop (power wasted as heat in the wires)—to ensure the final power network still delivers power reliably.
key_novelty: Deferring power delivery network design to after signal routing gives performance-critical signal routing priority for the backside metal.
contributions: BS-PDN-last design flow achieving 90% reduction in Total Negative Slack
12% performance gain with backside current distribution network (BS-CDN)
First comprehensive comparison of FS-PDN, BS-PDN, and multifunctional backside designs with vector-based analysis
